utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. We'll continue the procedures today. Witness, would you please stand up. Please make the solemn declaration in accordance with that paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what your name is.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sreten Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: P-e-t-r-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, were you a member of the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Potocari on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you were doing in Potocari on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was in hospital. On the 12th in the evening, I expressed a wish to go to Srebrenica. So they came to get me in the Zvornik hospital, transported me by car. I spent the night of the 13th. I said I wanted to go to Srebrenica because I had a flat there. We arrived as far as Potocari, and were unable to proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Friday we had a Prosecutor here, Ms. Issa, asking the question of why you didn't go back to the battalion and report yourself so you could go back on official duty. Could you please tell us why you didn't do that on July 13th.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know where the battalion was at the time, so I couldn't go. How could I go? They were transporting me by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your physical condition at that point in time, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded with two bullets in the left leg, above the knee, and in my right arm, forearm. They were entry/exit wounds. I had bled profusely, and I was very tired. I was exhausted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, one by one. Your leg, where exactly were you injured in your leg?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was hit in my left thigh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that there was an entry and exit wound?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Entry and exit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bullet hit any bones?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The bone was undamaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to walk without the assistance of a cane or someone?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, not in those first days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about your arm? You said that one of your arms had received a bullet as well. Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My right arm, my lower right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please demonstrate for us or show us where exactly. You don't have to take off your jacket, but if you could just stand up and --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was there an entrance and an exit wound?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Entrance and exit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Now, are you right-handed or left-handed?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm right-handed, completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So if you had a weapon, you would be using your right-hand -- your right hand at the trigger. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to hold a weapon without this arm, not in that condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you went to Potocari, were you in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us exactly what you did once you got to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I tried to get out of the car, but couldn't. We stayed there for a bit, then they took me out of the car because I said I wanted to get out to see what was going on there. I stood in front of the car for some ten minutes. After that, I got back into the car and we drove off to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, where did you receive your medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik, at the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 9th at 1800 hours. I arrived in Zvornik on same day, at around 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did -- when did you leave the Zvornik hospital?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As I said, on the 12th in the evening, at around 2100 hours, I expressed the wish to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the doctor's opinion with respect to your wish to check out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The surgeon was against it. I had to sign a document saying that I was leaving the hospital on my own initiative, of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After leaving that hospital in Zvornik, did you get any further medical treatment with respect to your wounds?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did. I had to go and have my wounds dressed daily and also receive an injection every day. After the third day, I was to go back to the surgeon for a check-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on July 13th, that is the day after you checked yourself out, did you go to any medical facilities to have your wounds dressed?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Bratunac health centre. That's where they dressed my wounds and gave me the injections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that before or after you went to -- towards Srebrenica when you stopped at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall now precisely whether it was before or after, but I think it was after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall being questioned in Banja Luka on the 29th of November, 2001? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether you were asked about being in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have had an opportunity to read your statement, have you not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did make a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but they provided the -- the translation was done on Friday, I believe, or Saturday. So that would have been the earliest that it had been provided to you by the Office of the Prosecution for you to review. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we finished, when I finished making my statement, I asked that they send me the recording and the photograph that they took of me. They promised to do that, but I never received that, nor did I receive any translation until Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Friday or Saturday? Because Friday I think you were still in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Saturday, yes, yes. Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in reading your statement, do you recall whether you were asked any questions with respect to being in Potocari on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall informing them at that point in time that you had been injured?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you provided them at that point in time with any documentation that would confirm, one, that you had received treatment at the Zvornik medical facility; and two, the injuries that you had sustained for which you were treated?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me for a document that would show I had been wounded. I had been wounded in 1993 also, so by mistake I gave them my letter of release from the military academy. Later on, I gave them the other document, the letter of discharge from Zvornik when I was wounded in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, in reading your statement it would appear that the -- that it was even translated into English by the interpreter at the time that you were questioned. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that can be found on page 17 of the statement. Now, let me show you what has been marked for identification purposes as 147. It's an untranslated, an untranslated, document. It's in Srpski. If you could please look at it first. Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the letter of discharge from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The date on the document is the 12th of July, 1995. I was admitted to the hospital on the 9th of July, 1995, and I was in hospital until the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the record, since we don't have it translated as of yet, if you could please read what it states, that short paragraph, which was translated or interpreted to the Office of the Prosecution when you were being questioned in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if there's a misunderstanding, but it was part of the Prosecution's case that this man was wounded. It's in Mr. Butler's report; it's in the documents. It's not in contest. I don't understand, you know, the point of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think there's no dispute between the parties concerning the wounding of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I was getting back to that good-faith basis that we heard on Friday. The good-faith basis was based on Ms. Issa's questioning as to why this man was in Potocari, why he didn't report to go on searching. And now what I'm demonstrating is the Prosecution, when they were questioning the gentleman on Friday, knew very well that this man was not ambulatory, was not able to walk. Yet nonetheless they wanted to give the impression to the Trial Chamber that he was the deputy commander in Potocari, as a presence, somehow lending to the ominous presence of the Bratunac Brigade being there. And what I'm trying to demonstrate is they knew very well as of Friday, in fact before that, that this gentleman could not walk, was merely there, and when you look at the report and you look at Butler's testimony, and you look at the line of questioning from the Prosecution, they don't put it into context. This man was there visiting. And we don't see that. We don't see that he was injured. We don't see that he could not walk. But we do see from his statement that the Prosecution knew about this. What I'm trying to demonstrate is there is very little good faith coming from that end and which is why I'm going through this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am absolutely appalled that this is a personal attack on Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's completely unjustified, it's unethical for him to be doing. It's a violation of the ethical rules of this Chamber. And it's just uncalled-for. But the point is that he is in Potocari and he is wounded; that is the point. And that he's in there because he has a great motivation to be there. That is the only point, and that has been the Prosecution's point all along. He certainly was questioned about his ability to report what he saw to his commander. This idea that now the Prosecution is on trial for not asking questions in good faith is absolutely absurd without justification and it should cease and desist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 65, Your Honour, line 1: "Would it be fair to say then that his injuries weren't so extreme" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. "Would it be fair to say then that his injuries weren't so extreme that he would be able to leave as the doctor discharged him and go to Potocari. Isn't that right." There is an answer. Next question: "Why wouldn't he come back to the battalion to help you in the middle of all that was going on at the time. Why was he still officially gone from the battalion?" These are the questions coming from the Prosecution on Friday. Had she read the document, had she read the medical report, all of which belonged to them and they had, one would know that this line of questioning is improper, because it suggests somehow that this gentleman was able to report for duty back to the battalion. And what I'm trying to demonstrate is all of this information was brought to the Prosecution's attention when the gentleman was questioned back two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I did not expect such a heated debate between the parties on Monday morning. Normally Monday is kind of a low day. And last Friday, I think the Trial Chamber made it very clear on the manners to conduct the direct or cross-examination, that is we should not concentrate on the attack of the other parties. We should concentrate on the case itself. In this situation, I believe there is no disputes between the parties; this witness was wounded. There's no dispute between the parties that this witness was in Potocari on the 13th of July. I think this is the common ground between the parties at this stage. As for how serious the person is wounded, there may be some different views. And you could possibly point out how serious this witness is wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I was doing that when I asked him to read from the section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But it is not necessary to attack the other parties on this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was merely bringing out their position on Friday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because we could compare the notes by ourselves at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that's why I told you that we haven't formed any opinions on this case yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was merely trying to be of assistance, Your Honour, but I take the point and I realise it is Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please read that one paragraph, so at least we know, because we don't have a translation version -- translated version yet. If you could please read it slowly now so it can be translated. And there may be some Latin terms which you may have to soldier through, I guess, in pronouncing them.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "Admitted because of tangential exit/entry wounds of the right upper arm -- right lower arm and left upper arm, sustained from firearms fired by the enemy during wartime operations in the area of Srebrenica." And then what follows is in Latin, and I can't really -- I'm sorry, but I don't really speak Latin. You could need someone with medical education to read this out and translate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And this document was provided to the Prosecution when you were questioned.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave it to them on the 29th of November, 19 -- 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, since we're talking about your injuries, let's stay with that. Could you please tell us when and where you sustained these injuries.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th at 1800 hours, I was wounded with two bullets, and these were entry/exit wounds. This was in the area of Kvarc Divljakinje, where the battalion was holding its positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, please tell us with which battalion and which battalion you were serving.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position in the 3rd Infantry Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the entire battalion or me personally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you personally. What was your -- you know, what function did you have? What title?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was deputy commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long you had held that position as deputy commander with the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, but I think it was in late 1994 or early 1995 that I was appointed. Before that, I had been wounded. I had been for rehabilitation, medical rehabilitation, and then I was appointed to this post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to cover that earlier period, but I thought we would get right to this area. Now, who was the commander when you were the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Mr. Dragan Zekic, and the brigade commander was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the -- I want to focus a little bit on the period when the events took place around Srebrenica, with ultimately Srebrenica falling on July 11, 1995. Now we do know that July 6th is when these events began. Could you please tell us on July 6th where you were located.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Between the 6th and the 7th, I was on Pribicevac. In the morning, I went to the right flank of the 3rd Infantry Battalion -- on the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long had you been in that position, prior to the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was, as I said in the beginning, for the battalion had been in that position from 1993, but I was appointed to my post in late 1994 or early 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Had the lines moved during that period?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, did you move your lines or your position?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, with your men, the ones that you were commanding at the time, fire any attacks toward the enemy?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the 7th? Did you advance at all?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th and the 8th, the fog was so thick that I could hear no attacks or detonations at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So does that mean that you did not advance?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We did not advance, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fire any -- fire at any targets?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's the 7th and the 8th. Now, let's get to the 9th, 9th of July. Do you advance at all?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any members of the 3rd Battalion that you were associated with move at all or did they maintain their entire position that they held from, say, July 6th?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th, the brigade commander, Vidoje Blagojevic, and I toured the right flank together. He ordered us to stay at the lines we had been holding before, but we had to put a few men forward to reconnoitre, to observe the movement of enemy forces, because we were expecting a possible counterattack from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th in the morning. We went 100 or 150 metres before the front line. We made some temporary protection barriers, because we had been told to expect bullets. And we stayed there. I was wounded there. We stayed there until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I was taken back to the vehicle after I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go step by step. So first of all how long -- when did you leave that area or how long were these observers at that area?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We were in the area on the 9th, up to the time when I was wounded we stayed there. After that, we withdrew, or rather, I was carried out. They remained at the line of the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say "we." Could you please explain to us who "we" is.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was with the squad, so myself and those ten men. And when I was wounded, they brought me out on a stretcher to the 100 -- 1.013th elevation point at Kvarc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this squad, did it belong to a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all members of the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were the Red Berets there by any chance?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the men, the ones that were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how many men exactly were there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: 10 to 15, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all in one location or had you spread them out?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We were in front of the line at a distance of perhaps 100 to 150 metres. We weren't grouped. We were spread out, 5 to 10 metres between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long had the Red Berets been part of the 3rd Battalion, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were attached to the 3rd Infantry Battalion as a reconnaissance platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was -- I'm sorry. Go ahead. Continue.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, that's when they were attached to the 3rd Infantry Battalion as a reconnaissance platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many Red Berets were there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, 20 at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many commanders did the Red Berets have?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, their komandir was killed at Krajina somewhere. I don't know the exact location. They were together, then they dispersed so that the ones that were attached in 1995 just had a deputy commander, komandir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who was that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was my son, Rade Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said those -- "the ones that were attached." Were there others, other Red Berets, that were not attached to the 3rd Battalion that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I know is that in 1992 a Red Beret company was established, and one or two months later they dispersed. Because the komandirs and deputy komandirs couldn't agree, so they dispersed. Twenty were left on this one side, and over there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the komandir or the deputy komandir of the other -- of the ones that were not attached to the 3rd Battalion, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: There was Prodanovic and his nickname was Mungo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Welcome. Did you Mungo during those days where you were?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us when you advanced with the 10 or 15 Red Berets, could you please tell us what sort of weapons, artillery, mortars, cannons, what have you, were available to you at that observation post.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My personal weapon, that is to say an automatic rifle, like all the ten men that were with me, side arms. We had no support and we didn't communicate with anyone or have any artillery pieces, no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you didn't communicate with anybody. Did you have any means of communication when you were there at that position on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a Motorola, and I could communicate with that Motorola with the battalion connections lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, behind you where the 3rd Battalion, your men had been stationed prior to you with the 10 or 15 going 100 to 100 [sic] metres forward as an observation post more or less, could you please tell us what kind of artillery was there to lend support to you.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any artillery pieces. They were just holding the lines and on guard in the trenches. They had no artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Drina Wolves there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. If you mean the axis I was at, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, where you were located. You didn't see Legenda and his Wolves?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were hit, were you in the process of attacking the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how was it that you were hit? What happened? Who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was our intention, since it was 1800 hours already, to go back to the line up there, where the rest of the battalion was located. And at the point of our return, I assumed the Muslim forces happened to notice us. And they showered us with a round of gunfire. And I was unlucky enough to be hit by two bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I take it after you left, from the 9th, and went to the hospital, you didn't engage in any more fighting during that period of time, that is on Srebrenica fell on July --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't even walk. How would I fight?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's start with some background information. Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Spat, Srebrenica municipality, and I lived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I live in Srebrenica today, in my flat, in the flat I lived in before our disagreements and conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. During the war, were you living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime towards the end of April or perhaps the beginning of May. I fled, I escaped from Srebrenica, simply stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said April or May, what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I went to the village where I was born, the village of Spat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is that from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you at that location?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was there -- we kept guard because we were afraid of an attack on the village. On the 8th of June, they did indeed attack us. And it is a village numbering eight houses. They attacked us. We had four wounded men, and my brother was killed in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then -- well, did you stay there or did you flee from there as well?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We stayed on there until the 12th of July, 1992, when they launched another attack. And then we had to withdraw down to the Sase mine to pull out. And that's where I was for a certain time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And from there, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They launched another attack, or rather, there were several attacks at the Sase mine. But on the 14th of December, there was an all-out fierce attack, so Bjelovac fell, and the other villages, the Serb villages, had fallen of course. And we had to withdraw from Sase, too, on the 15th to go to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this? What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The same year, 1992. The 15th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs were living in that area prior to that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Srebrenica and all that area that -- what was the percentage?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in Srebrenica municipality 30 per cent were Serbs, the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these villages that you spoke of? What was the breakdown, the ethnic breakdown?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were purely Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you went to Bratunac in 1992, at the end, in December, were you formally mobilised at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Bratunac Brigade had been formed, and I myself actually didn't receive any call-up. But of course I was forced to take part; I had to take part, even without that, to join the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exactly was it that you joined the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but I do know that upon arrival in Bratunac some of the men were sent to above Hranca, the village of Glogova, to take up there positions, where there was another attack, and about ten of them were killed, ten Serbs. And then after that, we got the line, Ladza, Pajici -- prior to the new year, Ladza, Pajici, Glogova, that's when we got that line. 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In which unit were you serving?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was the 4th Infantry Battalion. And I myself headed the battalion as the commander of the 4th Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what period are we speaking about?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're speaking about the 14th of December and the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you just please tell us very briefly the various positions you've held from that point in time until July 1995. What positions have you held with the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Within the Bratunac Brigade - as I said, at that time, I was the commander of the 4th Infantry Battalion - after my wounding the battalion was attached to the 9 -- in 1993 to the other battalions. So it was disbanded and two companies were attached to the 3rd Infantry, and one company remained in the 1st or 2nd Battalion, I don't remember, but I was undergoing treatment at the time because I had been wounded, in February actually, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what kind of wounds did you sustain in February 1993, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, an exit/entry wound in my left arm from a sniper, the upper arm above the elbow, and part of the elbow was smashed. And I got an entrance/exit wound through the right hip, also by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you on leave, recuperating, from your injuries?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was in Loznica and Zvornik in the hospital there, and then afterwards the medical military academy, the VMA. After I left the academy, I had to wear a fixation device on my arm and had to go for monthly check-ups to see the surgeon. So I had to go from Bratunac to Belgrade to the medical military academy to have my examination and have the extension removed. And then I had to go for spa treatment and rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it another way. When did you return to the Bratunac Brigade. You say you were injured in February 1993, so when did you return to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the end of 1994, or perhaps even the beginning of 1995. I really can't remember the date, but that was the general period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned, where were you placed within the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was still listed as an injured man of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. And I was deployed at the time as deputy commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what sort of training you received in order to become the deputy commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any military training, except for having served the -- in the Army of Yugoslavia doing my compulsory military service in 1974, 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you did your compulsory military service with the JNA, did you by any chance go to the reserve officer's training programme that was provided for some?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us in what capacity or what unit you served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I went as a young soldier to Krusevac, and I was recruited to the atomic, chemical, biological defence, the ABHO, as it was known. And after Krusevac, three months later, I was redeployed to Zagreb where I was at Borov Gaj [phoen], throughout the rest of my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you left your military service, as part of the All People's Defence I understand everybody was in the reserves, could you please tell us whether you were and if so what sort of unit you were serving in the reserves.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was within the civilian protection system in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after you did your JNA service, I take it you began working. Cold you please tell us just very briefly what do you do -- what were you doing prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had graduated from the mining vocational secondary school. I then went to the Yugoslav army. When I left the army, I went back and worked in the lead and zinc mine of Sase at Srebrenica, again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you supervising anybody there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: For a time, I was the shift supervisor, but afterwards, five or six years later, I was head of the pit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So at least before --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Foreman of the pit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before becoming the deputy commander, you had some sort of supervisory role over people?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the mine, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But in the field, as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, I was the deputy battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to the events - and I want to focus our attention a little bit closer to July 1995 - prior to the events on Srebrenica, were there any meetings held to at least notify you about the events that were ensue July 6th and onwards?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about any meetings, and I wasn't -- I didn't receive any notification of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, on July 6th were you told what the goals were that -- what was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you ever ask your commander, Mr. Zekic, or the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic, did you ask him what the objective was of this -- of these activities?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever told that you and your men had to advance to try to capture Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you ever come across any prisoners, any Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to this incident on Srebrenica that started -- or the events in Srebrenica, starting with July 6th, there was some -- there was an incident or there was some activities that had started a month or so earlier. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I'm specifically referring to around Jadar. Am I correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, did you participate in those events?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were on active duty at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what those events were about. What happened, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, with -- there were shifts replacing each other every seven or so days from certain lines, so that the Skelani battalion, part of the battalion, had a shift replacement. And at Osmaci, the Muslim forces had placed an ambush for that incoming shift and killed 13, 14, or maybe 15 men. I'm not sure of the number; I think it was approximately 15. And the UN checkpoint, we referred to it as UNPROFOR, was in Zeleni Jadar in front of the industrial zone there. And its task was to prevent events of that kind from taking place along the Zeleni Jadar/Skelani road, and of course the Zeleni Jadar/Bratunac road, too; however, ambushes did take place. When the Serb forces came to take up their shifts along those roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I want to go step by step, and this is a rather important area. Do you know about when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in June, the end of May, beginning of June. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ambush that was set off by the Muslim forces, could you please tell us how close that was to the UNPROFOR checkpoint that was there or observation point.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was on the road towards Skelani in the Osmaci region, underneath Osmaci, on the main road, asphalt road, underneath Osmaci. As to kilometres, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, is it very far, or is it nearby? Do you have any understanding of where the ambush was in relation to the observation post, where the UN was supposed to be there, not only to protect the citizens of the Srebrenica enclave, but to protect the Serbs from the Muslim forces that had not been demilitarised within Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Counsel is just testifying and said what the UNPROFOR mandate was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think we spent 30 minutes on those areas before Srebrenica on 12th of July already. I hope you get over this part as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, but keeping in mind that the Prosecution's theory is that this was a prelude to the attack on Srebrenica. This was the first step. This is what Butler advocates. This is what their star witness, Nikolic, has stated. And they make also reference to a debriefing from the Srebrenica report as well. So this is part of their theory, and I think, one, we need to put it into context; and two, get the gentleman's understanding of what he believed the June incident was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think there's no dispute that both parties during their time committed the serious crimes. And those instances were related to the attack on Srebrenica. But the attack itself is not a subject matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would agree with you in part, but when we have this joint criminal enterprise where they're saying the attack on Srebrenica was one continuous process --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, this is a discussion which I think it may be an interesting discussion to have for the Court at this point, but it shouldn't be done in front of the witness. We could do it very briefly; we also may have some agreements with counsel. But to tell the Prosecution what he believes the Prosecution's theory is in front of the witness, this may affect the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, the gist of my intervention is just to ask you to speed up your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to go as fast as I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Especially on this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the Muslim forces conducted that ambush, what was the response? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We were frightened. We expected to be ambushed at any moment or attacked from the back. We had to be at the ready all the time. We had been at the lines for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a counterattack or a response by the VRS forces as a result of this Muslim attack?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't carry out any attacks or any sort of retaliation, but above Jadar, above the UNPROFOR checkpoint, there was a wood we decided to take because we thought that between the Biljeg checkpoint and the Zeleni Jadar checkpoints, I'm speaking of UNPROFOR checkpoints that there was a free zone, that it was not under any kind of control. And that this is where the Muslim forces would pass through and ambush us. So we took that wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before doing so, do you know whether there were any negotiations to try to see whether the UN could find some sort of a way to get the parties, the Muslims and the Serbs to resolve this situation, short of military force?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I don't know if it was before the negotiations, but I did observe from that wood because we were some 20 metres above the UNPROFOR checkpoint. And I saw Momir Nikolic, a colonel from the corps, negotiating about moving the Zeleni Jadar checkpoint, asking them to go back to Ljubisavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Prosecution's in-house military analyst - and I say that with quotation marks - states here in his report on page 16, paragraph 138, he says, and I'm just going to read just one sentence:"With the political stage set, the initial military operation against the Srebrenica safe area began on 31 May 1995. VRS/Drina Corps forces launched Operation Jadar 95." Now, to your understanding, sir, this operation or counterattack as a result of the ambush from the Muslims, was this, to your understanding at the time, the first step to occupying Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We only concluded that this is where Muslim forces were passing through and we wanted to close off the area. We wanted to have control over that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Had that been the objective, that is a military objective, to take over Srebrenica, can you think of what operation might have -- what the operation might have looked at -- like or what territory they would have -- you would have tried to take over, to facilitate, that is, the second attack that occurred or started in July 6.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Zeleni Jadar is in a valley. It has no strategic dominance, so Zeleni Jadar would not have to be taken if we wanted to take Srebrenica. If we were going to attack Srebrenica, we should have taken the checkpoint on Biljeg, and cut the Srebrenica-Jadar communication at Ljubisavic, because from there, you can see all of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after that incident did you and your battalion do anything else in preparation for what was to occur, starting with July 6th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me read to you just before we leave this area what Momir Nikolic has testified to in court when he was being questioned by. Mr. McCloskey on 19th September 2003. It's open session. It's page 1.637, line 7. He's asked: "Did you become -- was there any official announcement of this attack plan after Zivanovic told you informally?" There's an answer: "I was not aware of any official announcement. I did not have an opportunity to see any official announcement, not in that sense that I had insight into accounts a complete set of documents related to the attack; however, in my position, I knew when preparations were underway for the attack on Srebrenica. Question: "When did the brigade start making preparations for the attack?" Answer: "Preparations began much earlier, much before the official date when everything became obvious. In my estimate, this is a personal assessment I'm giving you, the preparations began when the UNPROFOR checkpoint in Zeleni Jadar was attacked and when this checkpoint was taken. This is in late May or early June. Intensive preparations began in late June and early July." My question to you, sir, is: Is Mr. Nikolic correct in his assessment that the attack and the takeover of the UNPROFOR checkpoint was a preparatory attack in order to destroy or do away with the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised that such a high-ranking person should make this assessment. I'm sure he's wrong. The UNPROFOR checkpoint was something he personally negotiated to have moved peacefully so that we could control that area and that road. Had we been preparing to take Srebrenica, it would have been more logical and strategically important to bypass that checkpoint and take the one at Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just lastly, for those of us who are unfamiliar with that area, why was that piece of road so important to the VRS or to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It was important because we always felt unsafe, insecure, when we were changing shifts at the line. When we were going down that road, we were always afraid of an ambush because the Muslim forces were able to pass by that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to go into a bunch of documents, and maybe -- this may be a good time so that way I can just go through all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think we'll break here and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I want to show you now some documents before we return to the narration. Let me show you what has been marked as D144 for identification purposes. Please look at it; take your time. And I'm going to focus your attention on paragraphs 3, 4, and 8. All right. Now, do you know what this document is by looking at it, the top? Is it not an order?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This cannot be treated as an order. This is simply information for the unit commanders. These are suggestions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, does it not say: "Deployment" -- at the top "deployment of units in the defence region of the 3rd Infantry Battalion," and underneath it says: "Order."

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document and held it in my hands. As far as I can see up here it says: "Trisic." This document probably arrived -- was with the commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But is this not an order, though? Is it not -- does it not state: "Order"?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It does say "order," yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date is 4 June 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, looking at the very first paragraph before we got to the enumerated paragraphs, it states: "On the basis of clear need and for the purpose of completely closing the line, taking up combat positions, and organising the defence in the wider region of the village of Zeleni Jadar." And then the commander hereby orders several points, 11 to be exact. In light of your position as the deputy commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, do you know what this first part calls for?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please give us your opinion as to what is being called when it says that: "On the basis of clear need and for the purpose of completely closing the line, taking up combat positions, and organising the defence in the wider region of the village of Zeleni Jadar," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we closed off that part above the UNPROFOR checkpoint, the need arose because the 3rd Infantry Battalion did not have enough manpower to remain at that line. And then probably the commander estimated that other units should arrive there so that we can hold that line securely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to paragraph 3, it talks about your particular battalion, does it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph 3, it says: "The commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion shall task a leader of a company consisting of one platoon, each from the 1st 2nd, and 3rd Infantry Battalions, to occupy the defence region of the asphalt road between the village of Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica on the left, and Tucak on the right." Do you know whether this was accomplished, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area of responsibility of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and it was logical for the commander to issue an order that we should designate a komandir, a company komandir for those units, and this was done. Tucak was a dominant place; I think it was taken. And the wood towards Zeleni Jadar was -- well, the units that the commander ordered were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the komandir that was assigned? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Bozo Vuksic, that he was the company komandir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where is he from? Which unit?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He is from the 3rd Infantry Battalion, I think from the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we go to the next paragraph, number 4. It states: "The commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion shall incorporate this company in the battalion's control and command system and with the assistance of the brigade's chief of communication organise wire and radio communication with this company." First question: Was this done, to your memory?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us: Why would this be necessary? What is the significance of this particular task, in light of the order and the circumstances as they existed back then?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The units had to be ready so that they could communicate with the battalion command, and for that reason communications had to be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be normal or would that be an extraordinary task as sort of a prelude to some sort of ongoing -- some activity that was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. This was normal. Every unit normally had communications with its command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to point 8, it states: "The Red Beret platoon shall be held in reserve in the region of the 3rd Infantry Battalion command post to intervene along endangered axes." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all it says: "The Red Beret platoon," as opposed to a Red Beret platoon. To your understanding at that period of time, how many Red Beret platoons were there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Only they were the Red Berets at that time, and the ones that separated off from the Red Berets were called the Mungosi as far as I know. But only the ones attached to the 3rd Infantry Battalion were the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the Red Beret platoon, to your understanding, consisted of how many men?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: 20 people at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And that's the one that was -- the deputy commander was your son, Rade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, here it states that they shall be in reserve in the region of the 3rd Infantry Battalion command post. Now, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When we took that wood, it was logical to expect an attack by the Muslim forces. We had to have some men in reserve in case there was fighting. They were at Pribicevac where the battalion command was, and they were stationed there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they were physically located there, at least as of 4 June 1995, pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had been attached to or were part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion prior to this particular order, prior to this date, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to this last paragraph, just for point of clarification it says: "To intervene along endangered axes." Now, intervene, one would get the impression that this is some sort of an intervention platoon. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, it was an intervention platoon because they were to intervene along endangered axes. That's the reason for the name, intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when one hears of Red Berets, they conjure up images of some sort of a special force, sort of like the Green Berets of the American forces, or the real Red Berets that we've heard about from Serbia. What kind of an intervention platoon was this, really, since your son was deputy commander, and you were there on the line with him on 9 July 1995 when you got injured?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were only known by the red berets they wore in 1992. After that, they took them off and didn't even wear them, but the name stuck. They were just like other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. One last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't need the document anymore, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question. Your son, how old was he at the time when he was a deputy commander of the -- this intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe -- Mr. Karnavas has misspoken. I'm not sure whether he meant deputy commander. He was the commander, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. When the son was the deputy komandir, the son. I can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your son, Rade Petrovic, was he the commander or deputy -- was he the commander, komandir, or the deputy komandir of this intervention platoon, the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The komandir of the Red Berets was killed in the Krajina, I think in Drvar, and he replaced him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So was he -- was -- was his title komandir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they treated him, but I do know he was the deputy commander. He deputised for the komandir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave it at that. In any event, could you please tell us what his age was at the time back in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My son was a minor when the war broke out. At this point in time, he would have been 18 or 19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But he had some experience I take it, at least two or three years?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't have any experience. He hadn't even done his military service. How could he have gained experience? That's why he was wounded on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let me show you now -- just going right back. The Red Berets were at the command post and were in compliance with that particular order, to your understanding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was no need to intervene; they just remained stationary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you what has been marked as P416. And I'm going to be focusing on paragraphs 1 and on paragraphs 5. Do you recognise what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a report to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It's a daily combat report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably it is a daily combat report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the date is; it's at the top.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's illegible here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: On this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The English version states 10 July 1995. Let me go to the first paragraph. It states: "The enemy carried out combat activities all along the brigade defence line, in particular in the 3rd Infantry Battalion area of responsibility." Do you know whether this occurred on that particular day, this is the 10th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down to paragraph 5. It says here: "Sreten Petrovic, son of Ilija, (deputy commander of the 3rd Battalion) suffered serious injuries in the thigh and the forearm. " Now, that is your name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is your father's name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go down to the signature line, it states that this -- at the end of the page it says 10 July 1995 at 1740, which would be 5.40 in the afternoon, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is this correct, in light of the medical report that I showed you earlier, and of course your own personal knowledge of having suffered the injuries and having received medical attention?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But is this date correct? Did you suffer those injuries?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The date of my wounding, it's well known it was the 9th, at 1800 hours, not the 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But there's nothing here on this document that reflects -- at least if it was going to be an accurate document, there's nothing here that reflects that the injuries that you sustained had been sustained the day before, that is on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The report was probably a day late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The report to the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. But there's no correction as to when the injuries occurred, thus giving perhaps the impression that the injuries occurred on that particular day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know very well that it was the 9th. I was admitted to hospital on the 9th, as can be seen in the document from the hospital where I was treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let me show you another document. And this is P688. This has been admitted. Would you please look at this document, sir. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And have you seen it before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all what is this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on the appointment of the War Presidency of Srebrenica, and this was issued on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go down there on I believe it's number 4, it says: "Sreten Petrovic." Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Sreten Petrovic, deputy commander of the 3rd Battalion."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you told us earlier that you had been injured on the 9th of July. We know that you were spotted in Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995. And now we have this document that you have been appointed to the War Presidency of Srebrenica on 14 July 1995. Sir, could you tell us whether you attended any meetings, during which time you had put your name forward for this particular appointment.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did not put my name forward, and I don't know who put me on this list. But during those days, I was not able to attend -- I couldn't have attended any meetings because I wasn't able to move. And they didn't invite me to attend either during those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, on the 14th of July, 1995, that's the day after you had tried to get to Srebrenica but were unable to go past Potocari, where were you July 14th, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think that on the 13th of July I tried to reach Srebrenica because it was my wish to go to my flat in Srebrenica. As for the 14th, I don't know about that. I know that afterwards I went for treatment and back to my flat for a rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "flat," where was the flat for a rest? Are we talking about the Srebrenica flat or is there another flat as well?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. In Bratunac. I was accommodated in Bratunac temporarily in a flat in the Lamele area along the Bratunac/Konjevic Polje road, where the electrical distribution company is located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just one point of clarification, because I think I might have missed it during the first session. When you said you had a wish to go to Srebrenica, did that wish also include a wish to see the people that had been or that were in Potocari on that particular day, who had been there the day before as well?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Had I known that there were people in Potocari and that I wouldn't be able to pass through Srebrenica, I wouldn't have gone to Potocari at all. I did not have any wish. My only wish was to go to see my flat in Srebrenica, from which I had to escape in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can exclude you from the group of the curious that had -- that might have been in Potocari for those reasons?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've given you my reason, and that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you another document which has been marked for identification reasons as D145. Please look at it, spend a few moments. Look at the date on top and look at the name at the bottom. And of course give the rest a quick glance. All right. Now, what is the -- first of all, what is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The 13th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time, were you still convalescing, or had you returned to your position with the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think I had already recovered in this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that would have put you back on the front line or back at least within the fold of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Infantry Battalion at this point in time was, I believe, at Drvar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I had received an assignment from the brigade command when I returned and recovered that I should take part of the battalion which had not gone to take up its positions at Drvar to secure a campsite of Slapovici, a camping site at Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that. But first, at the bottom of the page of this document, it says: "Sreten Petrovic." It says: "On behalf of the 3rd Infantry Battalion commander, Sreten Petrovic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the document that I handed you, which was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution, does it have your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document that bears your name at the bottom of it, that states: "On behalf of the 3rd Infantry Battalion commander." Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the title of this document, it states: "The war history of the reconnaissance platoon of the 'Red Berets.'" Does it not state that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to coming here today, you have seen the document? I have shown it to you, have I not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was that the first time or had you seen it previously?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't shown to you, for instance, when you went to Banja Luka, when you gave them your documents, they didn't show you theirs?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at this document and you look at the points from 1992 all the way down to the bottom, which talks about 1995, were you aware of what the Red Berets were doing during that period of time, as it's stated in this particular document, that bears your name, albeit not your signature, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have known that. Where would I have known that from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who generated this document? Who was the person, the author, the creative genius behind this particular document that talks about the war history of the reconnaissance platoon of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, nor was I ever sent a document like this to certify and sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever, sir, a member of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did your son, perhaps, who had been the acting komandir, deputy komandir, did he sit down, perhaps, and narrate a history, the glorious history of the Red Berets for you to put your name to at some point in time as sort of an authentication of their bravery and their accomplishments during this period?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Had he written this, he would have probably authenticated it or sent it to me to authenticate. But I wasn't able to verify it because I didn't know their war history at all. My son was injured several times, and I'm sure that he doesn't remember all these dates, let alone me. So as for this document, I'm holding it in my hands for the second time, that is to say, when you gave it to me and now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, we can go on to the next document. And this one is D143. It has been admitted I am told. If you could -- this document, if you could look at the first page. Perhaps by looking at it you might be able to tell us what the document is.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But in looking at it you see several names, do you not, listed on this document? It's a compilation of names, and as you move from left to right at the last column there seems to be a designation as to where these names belong to, in which company, which battalion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
