utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to focus on a name -- there are two names there actually, but I'm interested in the first name, the first one that I've underlined for you. Miroslav Stanojevic. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The ERN number for this document, Your Honour, is 00658848. I don't see it -- there's no pagination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go all the way to the last column it says: "3 PB," which would mean 3rd Battalion, from what I understand. Correct? And then you see another word that's in brackets. Could you please tell us what that word means or stands for.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the word has just been disclosed. It says "crveni" in quotation marks, red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They used to call each other individually, say, "Crveni," Red, or some secret name. Maybe it was taken from the Red Beret name, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But this might denote that this gentleman was with the Red Berets, would it not? Because if we go up in the same page, if you just give it a look, you see "crveni" on several other names in quotes, do you not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could perhaps mean that, but perhaps not on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's assume that it does. I want you to make that assumption. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness indicated right at the beginning he doesn't know the document. Now he sort of doesn't know what he's -- what "crveni" means, and I'm just wondering if the witness is helpful in answering questions on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Karnavas, first of all you have to ask this question whether he knows what this document is, so as to establish the knowledge of this witness to this document. Otherwise, it will get us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go about it in another way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has maintained and has claimed that this particular gentleman, Miroslav Stanojevic, was a member of the Red Berets. Now, to your recollection -- first of all, do you know this man, the man that's designated here as part of being the 3rd Infantry Battalion with "red" in quotes? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I knew the man, but he wasn't with me within the Red Beret composition when we were at the forward command post in front of the battalion on the 9th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the Red Beret platoon?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that he was not or you're not aware of whether he was, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the Red Beret platoon was with you on the 9th of July, 1995, 100 or 150 metres --

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Miroslav Stanojevic was not there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the previous order, the previous order, that I showed you that dates back as early as 4 -- is it 4 June? 4 June 1995 -- I'm sorry. It was 4 July 1995. I'm sorry. I was correct the first time, 4 June 1995. That's D144. We talked about it earlier. Where the Red Berets were to be part of the intervention force there. And you stated that to your recollection the Red Berets were there with the 3rd Battalion as of this date, 4 June 1995. So my next question is: From 4 June 1995 until 9 July 1995, when you were taken off the battlefield, did you notice Miroslav Stanojevic among this intervention platoon that was being led by or commanded by your son?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That will be it for that document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document that has been -- that's come into evidence as D132. We've discussed it to some degree with other witnesses. Perhaps you might be able to shed some light. You were the deputy commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. Sir, did you ever see this document while you were the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it has a date on it, 4 July 1994. If I understood your testimony correctly, that might have been a time when you were still convalescing from your injuries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you return to the Bratunac Brigade, you indicated to us that you were put in the position of deputy commander. Right?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, surely if this information, which has been prominently displayed before us here in this trial, surely this would have been made known to you when you returned to the Bratunac Brigade in your position as deputy commander, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go back -- I want to focus your attention to paragraph 2, the latter part. And I'm going to quote, if you could follow along. It's on page 3 of the English version. D132. It states: "We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Now, as a deputy commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, were you ever told about this policy that's announced in Commander Ognjenovic's information dated July 1994?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not me personally. Now, as to Commander Ognjenovic, I knew him personally. I knew that he had large ambitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, if he had large ambitions and large appetites, he must have surely given orders for you to advance, move your positions, try to take Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's leading and he's just arguing his case at this point. The witness said he had not received it personally, and I think that's as far as it can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That also is speculation, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, when you returned, when you became the deputy commander, were you given any concrete orders to advance towards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any concrete orders for the expulsion of the Muslims from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says here: "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible." Were the Muslims there temporarily or had they been there, as you've indicated, prior to the war to the tune of about 70 per cent?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: They had been there before the war, too, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ognjenovic must have known that, the commander?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably he did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As you said, Mr. President, that's entirely speculative. The witness said before what he knew about the document, and the rest is pure speculation on the witness's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, it's a possibility that the commander did know that they had been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when Ognjenovic left and the new commander came in, Colonel Blagojevic, did he ever share with you and your immediate commander, Zekic, this information to tell you that there was going to be a continuation of this policy that Ognjenovic, previous commander, had announced in his information dated 4 July?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not with me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you did have an occasion to see Colonel Blagojevic prior to the events leading up to the fall of Srebrenica, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your meetings with Colonel Blagojevic, did he ever express this policy or any policy that the moment of truth was coming where the enclave was going to be dismantled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The same as before, it's entirely argumentative, the choice of words: "The moment of truth has been coming," I think it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this occasion I don't think so. Maybe there is some problem with the choice of the words, Mr. Karnavas, but the main gist of this question is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blagojevic, when he took over and when you would have contact with him, did he ever state that there had been some policy or that there were orders that you would be involved in that would result in the elimination of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to fast forward a little bit in period of time. In October 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're through with that. Thank you. And I apologise for not bringing it to your attention earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, October 1995, did there come a time when you came across some prisoners, some Muslim men that you took in as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we talk about that, first of all, prior to that period, prior to October 1995, were you engaged in any searching operations where you came across prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when were those occasions where you searched the terrain, if you recall? What dates?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the date, but I do know that from the command I was given the assignment to secure the settlement of camp Slapovici, but those people two or three days later noticed that they were having night visitors in that camping site of Slapovici. And I ordered them not to open fire but just to observe. They were frightened. They thought they were strong Muslim forces that had remained behind in the hills and forests around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, where is this location, Camp Slapovici? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the left bank of the river Zeleni Jadar, not far from Zeleni Jadar proper, the industrial zone there which is about 4 kilometres to 5 kilometres away from the industrial zone called Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that the assignment was to secure the settlement. What does that entail, securing the settlement?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Through force of circumstance, the settlement was complete without inhabitants, of course. But the other people wanted to loot and pilfer and destroy it, demolish it, and to take away any of the goods they needed. In simple terms, to steal from the settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you said that you went there. Now, who was staying at that location? You said: "Those people two or three days later noticed that they were having some visitors." Who are those people?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were some elderly people and members of the 3rd Infantry Battalion who were not able to go on assignment to Drvar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were exhausted, didn't have any strength left, they might have had some family problems. Anyway, they stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went to secure this location, how many men went with you?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This -- for the security of the Slapovici camp settlement, there were two shifts, ten days each, eight to ten men in each shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you would do one shift and then somebody else would take out -- take over the next shift?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in charge of both shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you would remain and the other men would just be replaced?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there with the men all the time. I would bring the shift there, leave them there, go to Bratunac, and then I would visit them every two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how is it that you came across some prisoners while you were up there?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When my men informed me that there were night visits to the camp settlement of Slapovic, I knew that for the safety of those men and in order to carry out the task fully, we had to search the wider area of Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you search the wider area?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did carry out the search of the wider area of Slapovici. On the first day, we didn't find any traces; all we found were trampled meadows, old footprints that were a month or more old. In the evening on our way back to the camp, near the camp, there is a pine wood. And there we heard a dog barking. From my personal experience, I know that a dog without its owner does not bark. And this was a sign that there was somebody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all could you describe to us the manner and method in which you searched the terrain, so at least we can visualise how the search was done.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I heard the dog barking, it was already night. We got back to the Slapovici camp, spent the night there; and on the following day, in the morning, at 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning perhaps, we blocked all the entrances, the paths leading in and out of the wood. A Muslim called Refik who knew me personally came along, he knew me, I didn't know him. He was scared. I told him not to be afraid and not to flee. He didn't try to flee. I asked him how many other men were there; he said there were six others. We asked if he would lead us there; he said he would. The rest of my men gathered around. He took me to their camp. There were two others there; one of them was his brother Sefik. The other was an older man; his name was Nezir Djozic, and I knew him. Well, I didn't really know him, but I'd heard of the name before the war because he was well known in the area We went into their camp. They had pistols and hand grenades, so we disarmed them. We asked if there were other Muslims in the woods. They said there were others, but they were 500 metres away. Refik decided to take us there and we set out all together. We found those four men asleep in their camp; they were young men. One of them had been wounded, I'm not sure, but I think it was in the arm. So we took them to the Slapovici camp, loaded them on a vehicle, and brought them to the Bratunac Brigade, where we handed them over to Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go into what happened once you handed them over, I want to go back and ask you if you could clarify the one question that I asked. The day before you actually found these men, the day when you heard the dog barking, you indicated that you were searching the terrain. What I would like to know is how you searched the terrain, what method did you use? How were the men positioned as you searched the terrain?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we moved in threes and searched the terrain in sections, section by section. However, I wasn't expecting them to be in the wood nearby, the Muslims. We thought they were further away, so we went further away from our base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I take it you didn't march in column?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you took the prisoners and you handed them over to Momir Nikolic. First of all, why would you hand them over to Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic was in front of the headquarters when we arrived, and he received them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific orders as to who I should hand them over to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you see those men later?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. When I handed them over to Momir Nikolic, he took them to the canteen. We had breakfast together, not at the same table true to say, but I know the food was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you were able to observe them eating breakfast?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that point on, do you know what happened to the men or where they went?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them; I didn't ask. All I know is that one of them was among the first people to return to Srebrenica, Nezir Djozic. I see him now every day. I didn't know him before, but I know him well now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Incidentally, did you ever receive any orders from your commander or from Colonel Blagojevic to kill any prisoners that you came across?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. Had I received such an order, I would not have carried it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this searching operation, the one that you talked about where you're up there securing Camp Slapovici, were you involved in any other searching operations to try to locate whether there were other Muslim men that had not made their way from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Finally I want to show you a document that was faxed to me yesterday afternoon. I know you looked at it briefly. I only have the Serbian version, but I want you to look at it. It's my only copy, unfortunately, but if you could just look at it. And take a couple minutes. First of all, do you see your same in that particular document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I marked it so you could see it. And do you see the name of the individual that's mentioned in there that reportedly has made this report? Further up. It's the first page, the first line -- the first part that's marked.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, what's the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The -- this document for identification purposes will be 147, D147.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us the name of the individual -- first of all, what is this? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement. This is a record of a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the person who has made this statement, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And for the record what is his name?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: His name is -- his last name is Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That will be enough. When was the last time that you saw this individual?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your relationship with this particular person? And by that I mean how well do you get along with him or don't get along with him.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Adem Ademovic used to work in that zinc mine where I used to work. He was a colleague of mine on the machine side to be sure, but we knew each other very well. We met in Srebrenica ten days ago. We shook hands; we chatted for a bit. We invited each other for a drink, but he said he didn't have time so we parted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this particular document your name has come up with respect to certain activities back in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in the activities, were you personally involved in the activities that are referenced in this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps if we go into more detail, namely locations, I would suggest to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't planning on going into any more details, but if the Prosecutor wants me to go into details, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe on the safe side we should go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. I have no further questions. I appreciate your honesty in answering all of my questions. There may be some questions from Mr. Jokic's attorney, the Prosecution I'm sure, and perhaps the Judges. If you could be as forthright and as honest as you have been with me, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Lukic, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's almost time for a break. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to go back to the issue of the UNPROFOR checkpoint at Zeleni Jadar. You remember having talked about this this morning?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that you didn't carry out an attack, that you just went into a free zone, and I think you said you took a wood.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these days was this UN checkpoint actually attacked, and they have -- the UN people have to abandon it?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. We were in the woods for three days and Momir Nikolic was down there with the corps colonel, and they negotiated so that they could hand it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the negotiations successful? Was it handed over?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the UN checkpoint remained the way it was?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read then what the Dutch reported about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's P851, a report by DutchBat. It's been quoted several times, I believe by the Defence, cross-examination of UNPROFOR witnesses. It's on page 15, paragraph 247. And I would like just to read four lines. "On 1st June, the BSA, Bosnian Serb army, demanded that the battalion move OP Echo, enabling unrestricted use of an important road in the area of the OP. When the battalion refused to meet the demand on 3rd June OP Echo was attacked by the BSA, using hand-held weapons, motors, and anti-tank weapons. OP Echo was surrendered and two new OPs were immediately set up to take over the task of OP Echo." Now, does that refresh your memory as to whether the UNPROFOR checkpoint was attacked or not.

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that it was the classical type of attack. We did receive an order from Momir Nikolic, that's true, to simulate an attack. That means with infantry weapons to open fire but to fire into the air, strong firing up into the air and not at the UNPROFOR checkpoint. So these are two different concepts, whether it's an actual attack, a proper attack, or a simulated attack, so it was not an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in our saying, you used, in fact, weaponry, but in your opinion or your assessment, you fire into the air?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: We fired into the air. Our intention was, according to the agreement reached, that since they didn't wish to hand their checkpoint over we wanted to frighten them. And it bore fruit. Had the checkpoint remained there, we would have remained at our positions and I don't know what would have happened next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the checkpoint was, in fact, moved, contrary what you told us just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that it was not an attack. And to this day I consider that it was not an attack. As to the checkpoint, after they were frightened, they came out and attacked a point 200 metres from the first checkpoint they were at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points. Re-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sticking with that same document, P851, this report, which is the report based on debriefing on Srebrenica, and it's dated 4 October 1995, not to be confused with the NIOD report. It goes on to say where counsel left off that: "OP-E was surrendered and two new OPs were set up to take over the task of the OP-E." And then it states: "From then onwards, DutchBat was no longer able to disarm BiH soldiers, as there was ultimately no cooperation whatsoever from the local authorities (including the local civil police)." And that's in the same paragraph. My question is: Had the DutchBat been disarming or had they disarmed the BiH soldiers in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of whether there was any disarming, but what I do know is that the Muslim forces behind our lines set up ambushes and killed the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to read from another report, another Dutch report, the NIOD report, the one that we quoted last week. This was a report done by the Dutch government regarding the fall of Srebrenica. I'm referring from -- I'm reading from chapter 5. I'm going to read this section, and please -- I'm going to ask you to comment on it. It says here: "The Bosnian Muslims were in agreement regarding the VRS objective of capturing OP Echo. The use of the road link with Milici, the closure of the link between Zepa and Srebrenica, and gaining access to the bauxite mines. With the occupation of Zeleni Jadar as mentioned that the VRS also had the southern access to Srebrenica in their hands. According to Ramiz Becirovic, the commander of the ABiH 28th Division, there was no direct connection with the latter attack on the enclave, however. There were provisions -- there were provocations by the ABiH all the time. And the VRS had responded to it since December 1994. At the start of the actual attack on Srebrenica on 6 July, Becirovic also assumed that the only objective of the VRS was to further open the road from Zeleni Jadar to Milici. Osman Suljic also thought that the objective of capturing OP Echo was to enable the free use of the road from Bratunac to Milici. And underlying reasons seen by the intelligence staff of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla was that the ABiH was supplied from Zepa via Zeleni Jadar and the VRS wanted to bring an end to that situation. Within sector north-east, the staff likewise thought that the issue was the use of the road. It shortened the east/west links from the VRS considerably. It increased the possibility of keeping the population in the southern part of the enclave under control, of keeping an eye on the factory complexes to the south of OP Echo, of restricting the traffic to Zepa and of exercising control on the bauxite mines, which were said to belong to the vice-president of the parliament of the Republika Srpska. Civil affairs officer Ken Biser said that he had been proclaiming for a year that the VRS wanted to wrest control of the road concerned." Now, sir, having read that to you, this is from the Dutch government, do you have an opinion as to whether Ramiz Becirovic, the commander of the ABiH, 28th Division, was correct when he stated that the incident that happened in June was not directly connected with the later incident in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz was right. He probably wasn't connected to that on the 6th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it states here that the whole purpose was to take control over that piece of the road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the road to be safe and secure and for us to have control over that line of communication, that's why that was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked whether you attacked UNPROFOR. Did the Serb forces, the VRS, or your unit, did they ever fire directly at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this question is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR ever fire back at the VRS, as their rules of engagement might have allowed them to do so?

utterances.speaker: SRETEN PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. They didn't return fire from the checkpoint either, but they were collected up the weapons, got into an APC, and withdrew from the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. D144, which is the order, deployment of the units in the defence region of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, dated 4 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it should be June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be June. You're absolutely correct. I keep making that mistake. Absolutely. Thank you. D145, the War History of the Reconnaissance Platoon of the Red Berets, that was dated 13th September, 1995; 147, the letter of discharge for Sreten Petrovic. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Again, if we receive a translation of the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think I have received the translation during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I wasn't informed. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you -- if the Prosecution hasn't received it, I think it's an obligation for the Defence to furnish the translation to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have, Your Honour. I wasn't aware that they had received it, but apparently everybody has received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These three documents are admitted into the evidence. Are there any on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's Prosecution Exhibit 851. Mr. Butler has made reference to it a number of times and you had ruled not to admit it when it came in as a bunch. But again today it was on the list of exhibits for this witness from the Defence side, it wasn't used. But we used it and we believe it would be a useful document for Your Honours to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's a big document and we just made reference to one portion of it. And obviously if we're going to admit this, I have to find a way of going through every statement and maybe bringing a bunch of DutchBat folk over here to contest each and every portion of it. Now, I don't object to the one relevant portion that was read, which was paragraph 2.47. But to have the entire document puts an inordinate burden on the Defence of having to challenge now everything that's in the document, you know, just as I'm not putting forward the entire NIOD report, I'd like to, it's about 8.000 pages. But I think to the extent they make reference to this, I think that those relevant portions certainly can be admitted and we have absolutely no objection to that. But the entire document, that's another matter. Unless they want to lay proper foundation. They can bring in a witness through their, I guess, re-direct -- or their rebuttal case to lay the foundation. This is just a report based on briefings. So -- and we didn't hear from the rapporteur. We certainly haven't heard how this document was created, but for the purposes of making references to various portions, obviously I have no objection, but the entire document, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think that document has to be absolutely true to the facts. Just like the documents we admitted before, we don't believe that some documents say the truth. But so long as it has some probative value and as long as it's relevant to this case, we could admit them into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Generally I would say yes, generally, I underscore that. Specifically, I would have some problems with that, because one I'm being given a rather short period of time to put on my defence. And now I'm being burdened with, if this document comes in, of having to challenge everything, because I don't know where perhaps somebody might anchor a particular paragraph in this report, and say: "A-ha, it's in this report, therefore it must be true," and then they use this as a basis for anchoring another portion of some other conclusion. So if you want to admit it, that's very well; I've stated my objection. On the other hand, I will probably go over it with a toothcomb and it may require, it may require, it may require me to bring in some further witnesses to discuss this. Now, hopefully if we get Colonel Karremans here, as I'm trying to, the Dutch government will need some cajoling, but if we get him in here, of course, I can discuss this very thoroughly with the gentleman, as with the NIOD report as well. But at this point in time my basic fundamental fear is that there are things in this report that someone may latch on to, whether it be in one of the footnotes in Mr. Butler's report and he makes reference to this, or somebody later on, they hear a witness and say: "Ah, now we have circumstantial evidence, now we even have direct evidence, because it comes in this report," and all of a sudden something that is marginally, if at all, being proved is being given credence and weight in this trial as the basis of a report that has not even been -- the foundation has not been laid by the Prosecutor. So that's part of my problem. Again, I don't mind snippets of it coming in, when appropriate, as in this case. It was quite fair for Mr. Waespi to make reference to this report as a means of trying to impeach the gentleman, in anticipation. That's why I didn't use it. You notice I even have it marked. I have my own report, the NIOD, and I have the appropriate sections singled out. So that's my position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the consultations with my colleagues, we decided not to admit this document at this stage, but we believe that in the future proceedings this document will be frequently quoted and used. And before the Defence case is closed, we'll consider the admission of this document, all together with all the evidence we heard through the various witnesses. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps to assist you in that, I think the Prosecution will go through Mr. Butler's report, see where he has cited it, and perhaps there are some other small sections that you may consider in part of your overall opinion for your final decision on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Anyway, this issue is still pending, it's still pending. We did not say that we refused to admit it into the evidence and we did not say we admit it into the evidence at this stage. But anyway, before the closing of the Defence case, we'll consider the admission of this document once again. I hope at that time the Prosecution could remind us about the pending issues. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am ready, but -- I am ready, but the next witness apparently -- yesterday was rather tired and in my frank opinion, even though he's waiting in the wing, I would prefer that we have a little more time to meet with the gentleman before I put him on the stand. Coming to The Hague, he's quite anxious and was rather tired yesterday, so I wasn't able to spend too much time with the gentleman. In due deference to his needs - I'm prepared to go forward - but I would appreciate it, if at all possible, that we start with this gentleman tomorrow. For this week we have six witnesses. I don't think that there will be any problem in covering all six of the witnesses. I think tomorrow if I had the opportunity to meet with the gentleman a little bit more, I could be much more efficient, and tomorrow I believe we might even finish with two witnesses or close to that. But I think two witnesses is very possible. But this week we have six, again I leave it up to the Court's discretion. If you wish for me to start, we can, though I would prefer to have that little extra time. And I apologise for not being able to prepare the gentleman more thoroughly, but again they're coming over here, they have anxieties, I don't want to be pushy. So -- and I think Mr. McCloskey is fully aware of sort of the problems witnesses have at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we're on schedule and we're going to finish up, we don't have any problem with this. And I -- let me just offer perhaps a suggestion you may not want to consider, but the issue of the Zeleni Jadar checkpoint is an issue that I think Mr. Karnavas and I have -- can agree to disagree and that it does have some relevance in our view to Mr. Blagojevic. And I -- it's one of those many, many issues that may never fully get argued by the time we get to the end of the case or it may be left to the actual paper argument. And I think it's going to be an issue that's relevant in his future witnesses. Perhaps Mr. Karnavas and I could identify the issue for you in a -- I could speak for 3 minutes on it and he could speak for 3 minutes, that way you would see the issue as we see it. I don't know if you want to listen to us anymore and I certainly would understand if you want to see as the issue goes. But with a trial that's this long, it's so impossible to try to argue all the issues. This is -- and I thought perhaps something we could do to take up a little bit of the time, and I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, do you agree with the suggestion put forward by Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I'll try to maintain my thoughts within three minutes. I think that's possible. I could speak for about three hours on the issue, but I'll keep it short to three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all I would like to say that this Trial Chamber would only take into the evidence the testimony of the witnesses and other documents we admitted through other means like the 92 bis. I know that the parties have different views and positions on certain issues, and whatever the party claimed or alleged is not the evidence. Having said that, and I hope both parties will bear that in mind. Who will start for the three-minute presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I offered this programme. If you could please interrupt me in three minutes and we can do the same thing and wrap it up. I will really just speak about the issues and I hope to not argue too much. I wasn't prepared, so this is coming a bit off the top of my head. It is my understanding from reading some of the 65 ter and listening to the Defence that the Defence will be -- that Colonel Blagojevic was really unlucky in that he was in the wrong place at the wrong time and that he was -- just happened to become commander on May 25th and that he wasn't really listened to by various commanders. And it's the position of the Prosecution, as was referenced in Mr. Butler's report, that the attack on the enclave, which we know is July 6th, which really was preceded by the attack on OP Echo, which was the Zeleni Jadar checkpoint, which happened May 31st, and you heard about this negotiation to get rid of it. Therefore, it's our position that by May 31st, there was clearly an plan afoot to attack the enclave and take it out, and that Colonel Blagojevic's appointment on May 25th was done at a time when the Drina Corps staff was fully engaged in preparing plans and thinking about attacking the enclave. So they had him in mind during the attack. And so that's why I think this is an important issue for the Court to understand. We have two different viewpoints on it. And regarding the last point that was made regarding the OP and the road between Zeleni Jadar and Milici, if you remember there are two objectives to the Drina Corps attack plan. One is to separate the two enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa, Zepa being south, this road being right between the two enclaves, separate them because there is this line of communication where there's smuggling going on and the BiH have troops there that are able to do ambushes, like we heard. The legitimate military objective was to stop that, cut them in half and stop that so that doesn't happen, that's one objective; the second is to reduce the size of the enclave to its urban area, that being the more, as you know, insidious objective, from our viewpoint. And so that the Zeleni Jadar attack is part of objective number one, so they can reduce those attacks, and it happens to be right in the avenue of the attack and the preparation area. So it really interfered with the VRS plans to get ready and to prepare for that attack. And that -- this was something that needed to be done in order for the overall attack on the enclave to occur, and that it happened at a very similar time that Colonel Blagojevic was appointed. So that's the issue. Those are the points. That's why we have been responding with the questions that we have, and I know it's an issue that Mr. Karnavas is arguing as well from the other viewpoint. That's all I needed to say in my three minutes. And I hope that -- and I know you will listen to the evidence on these points as they come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's exactly three minutes. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll give it a shot. Well, part of the problem with drafting the indictment the way it's drafted is it covers this historical context. And they're anchoring what happened to what -- the events of July 1995 back to as far as 1992, more specifically to this area, however, if you look at Butler's testimony you will see that he uses Krivaja 95, which was drafted much earlier. And then they use the Jadar incident as a prelude to Srebrenica, as if Srebrenica -- the total elimination of the enclave was the goal. We all agree, or I think we have, that the attack on Srebrenica was not a crime. However, from there, the Prosecution's argument has been that while the attack was not a crime, what ensued thereafter, the humanitarian crisis and the evacuation was actually a forcible transfer, which originated its genesis was back as far as early 1992. So more or less when we see the Krivaja 95 and then we see the events of July 1995, it is more or less pregnant with this objective to eliminate the enclave, albeit when we look at the concrete orders it is very clear that it is not the elimination of the enclave, but rather it is to shrink the enclave, both Zepa and Srebrenica, because there had been quite a bit of smuggling of weapons going on, it wasn't demilitarised, there were lots of attacks and so on and so forth. If we look at the NIOD report, the section that I read has been consistent with what our position has been. And also the NIOD report makes reference to Major Nikolic -- they say Major Nikolic because he was representing himself to be everything but his true rank, which was captain. But you see that Major -- that Nikolic was negotiating, and the whole purpose of this was to try to find some resolution where the Muslim forces would not be committing these ambushes. So our position is you have two different incidents; one is not connected with the other. And that Colonel Blagojevic obviously had the luck or lack thereof to appear at the scene right before these two incidents. And it's been our position that he has never been involved in any of the activities, either before, during, or after. He wasn't involved in any forcible transfer. He wasn't involved -- his troops were not involved in the attack on Srebrenica or to eliminate the enclave, even as late as the 10th or 11th, that he wasn't involved in hunting down anybody who was on their way to Tuzla in order to capture them and to kill them. And so that's been our position. And I think that the Prosecution has been making their argument that Jadar and the attack on Srebrenica on the 6th are interconnected. And it's -- that's why it's necessary, for us at least, to be able to mount a defence to show that there perhaps may be other reasons, reasons that the Dutch government in its very comprehensive NIOD report has concluded through ABiH commanders that one was not related to the other. The Prosecution believes otherwise. That's their belief; they're entitled to it. They can try to prove it, and of course we are trying to do the opposite. That's why when we get to this particular issue, while it may not be directly on point with what happened after the fall of Srebrenica, because it's part of the Prosecution's case and part of their case as it relates to the forcible transfer issue and the ethnic cleansing issue, I think that we need to have a certain amount of latitude in order to mount a defence. Because I'm already anticipating their closing argument. I can deliver it for them, in fact. And that's why, knowing what I'm about to hear on closing, I'm slowly trying to anticipate that and fire back with my own ammunition in order to establish that they have no case, and they certainly can't prove it beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I said before, the statement by the parties is just the expression of the views they hold on the particular issue, and it has no evidential value at all. And we'll base our findings on the live testimony of the witnesses and other documents admitted through other means. Well, thank you very much. I think the hearing is adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.08 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
